Common
KOM-un
adj. (shared by all; also, ceremonially unclean, profane; rendering Greek koinos)
From Latin communis, shared. The Greek koinos holds both senses at once, and the collision of the two is the whole drama of Acts 10 — the same word means shared and defiled, because what is open to everyone is not set apart.

Biblical Definition

Common in the New Testament carries two senses that the book of Acts deliberately collides. In the ceremonial sense it means profane, not set apart, and therefore unfit — Peter's protest on the housetop uses it as a technical term: “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean” (Acts 10:14). The answer he receives abolishes the category by divine act rather than by argument: “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” (Acts 10:15), and the vision is repeated three times because Peter is about to walk into a Gentile house and needs to know that the barrier came down from heaven and not from his own liberality. In the other sense common means shared, and the same root describes the church's life: “all that believed were together, and had all things common” (Acts 2:44), and Paul greets Titus as his own son “after the common faith” (Titus 1:4), while Jude urges contending for the faith once delivered, having intended to write of the common salvation. The two senses are joined by the same Greek word koinos, from which comes koinonia, fellowship. What God has cleansed becomes shareable; the removal of the ceremonial barrier is exactly what creates the common life of Jew and Gentile in one body.

Webster 1828 Definition

Both shared and profane, from one Greek root. Peter refuses what is common or unclean and is told not to call common what God has cleansed; the same word gives the church its common faith, common salvation, and all things common.

expand to see more

COMMON, a. [L. communis.] Belonging equally to more than one, or to many indefinitely; as, life and sense are common to man and beast.

2. Belonging to the public; having no separate owner; as a common field.

3. Usual; ordinary; frequent.

4. Of no rank or superior excellence; ordinary; vulgar.

5. In Scripture, unclean; profane; not consecrated. Call not thou common. Acts 10.

Key Scripture

Acts 10:14 — "But Peter said, Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean."

Acts 10:15 — "And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common."

Acts 4:32 — "And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common."

Titus 1:4 — "To Titus, mine own son after the common faith: Grace, mercy, and peace, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Saviour."

Modern Corruption

Acts 10:15 has been lifted out of its dietary and Gentile-inclusion setting and made a general principle that no one may call anything unclean — a warrant for affirming whatever God has plainly called sin.

expand to see more

“What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” is now regularly deployed as a proof-text for the affirmation of behaviours Scripture forbids: God has cleansed, who are you to call it unclean? The move ignores what the vision was about and what Peter himself said it was about. He interprets it in verse 28 — God has shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean — and the referent is Gentile persons, previously barred by ceremonial law from table fellowship. The abrogation is of the ceremonial code that separated Jew from Gentile, which the whole New Testament teaches was a temporary partition (Ephesians 2:14-15). It is not an abrogation of the moral law; the same apostles who received this vision wrote the epistles that name idolatry, fornication, and covetousness as excluding from the kingdom. God cleansed the meats and admitted the Gentiles; He did not repeal the seventh commandment.

The all things common of Acts 2:44 is corrupted in the parallel way, cited as a scriptural mandate for compulsory community of goods. Luke's own account resists it. The selling was voluntary and occasional, distribution followed need rather than equality, private ownership continued — Peter tells Ananias plainly that the land was his own and the money in his own power (Acts 5:4), so that his sin was lying and not withholding — and the practice belongs to a particular moment in Jerusalem. What the passage does establish, and what wealthy churches evade more often than they admit, is that a Christian's property is genuinely at his brother's disposal when there is need. That is a stiffer standard than most who cite the verse and most who dismiss it are living by.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek koinos (common, shared; hence ceremonially profane) and koinoo (to make common, defile); the same root yields koinonia, fellowship, and koinonos, a partner.

expand to see more

Greek koinos (G2839) — common, shared; in the ceremonial sense, unhallowed or defiled; the word in Acts 10:14, Acts 2:44, and Titus 1:4.

Greek koinoo (G2840) — to make common, to defile; the verb in Mark 7:15 and Acts 10:15 (call not thou common).

Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, communion, sharing; the same root, and the church's word for its shared life.

Greek akathartos (G169) — unclean, impure; the companion term paired with koinos in Acts 10:14.

Hebrew chol (H2455) — profane, common, not holy; the Old Testament counterpart, opposed to qodesh (holy) in Ezekiel 44:23.

Usage

"“What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” — the ceremonial barrier removed by divine act, not human liberality."

"“Had all things common” — voluntary, need-driven, and in a particular hour; property was still owned."

"“After the common faith” — the one faith shared by Jew and Gentile, which the vision made possible."
